title: How general anaesthetic drugs switch off the brain
ariaLabel: Schematic of consciousness: excitatory glutamate signalling through NMDA receptors keeps the brain aroused, and inhibitory GABA signalling through GABA-A receptors quietens it. Propofol and thiopentone-type drugs strengthen GABA-A inhibition, ketamine blocks NMDA receptors, and volatile agents act on several channels including GABA-A.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Glutamate
nodes.info: The main excitatory signal of the brain acting on NMDA receptors.

nodes.label: Volatile agent
nodes.info: An inhaled anaesthetic agent that has reached the brain.

nodes.label: Wide quieting
nodes.info: Quieting of neurons across several systems.

nodes.label: Consciousness
nodes.info: A teaching score for the level of consciousness, set by excitation and inhibition in the brain.

edges.label: GABA-A receptors
edges.info: Propofol, thiopentone and etomidate-type drugs strengthen the chloride current of GABA-A receptors, which quietens neurons.

edges.label: NMDA receptors
edges.info: Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor channel. This causes dissociative anaesthesia rather than classic sedation.

edges.label: multiple channels
edges.info: Volatile agents act on several targets, including GABA-A receptors, glycine receptors and two-pore potassium channels, so the effect is drawn as one enhancing step.

sources: Where each class acts. Propofol and thiopentone-type drugs strengthen GABA-A inhibition, ketamine blocks NMDA receptors, and volatile agents act on several channels including GABA-A. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Nitrous oxide, opioids and muscle relaxants in anaesthesia, MAC and partition coefficients, uptake and distribution, dexmedetomidine, haemodynamic and respiratory effects, malignant hyperthermia, depth monitoring and adverse effects are left out. Consciousness is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
